chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS soft­ ware (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Within-group comparisons of baseline and 12-month BCVA were performed using paired t-tests. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The association between injection number and visual acuity change was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Treatment switching Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept was considered in eyes demonstrating inadequate ana­ tomical or functional response. Inadequate response was defined as persistent retinal fluid, insufficient ana­ tomical improvement on OCT assessment, or lack of satisfactory functional improvement, as judged by the treating physician, despite repeated injections. Because of the retrospective real-world design, no rigid quanti­ tative anatomical or visual acuity thresholds were pre­ defined; treatment switching decisions were based on the treating physician's overall clinical judgment integrat­ ing both anatomical and functional response. For eyes undergoing treatment switching, the timing of switching, BCVA before switching, and BCVA after switching were recorded. Treatment switching was unidirectional from bevacizumab to aflibercept during the 12-month study period; no eyes switched back to bevacizumab or under­ went additional therapeutic modifications. Multivariable linear regression To identify independent predictors of visual outcomes, a multivariable linear regression analysis was per­ formed. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR). Independent variables included baseline BCVA, total number of injections during the first year, and treatment switching status. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and prior literature. Regres­ sion coefficients (β) and corresponding P values were reported. Generalized estimating equation analysis To account for potential inter-eye correlation arising from inclusion of both eyes from some patients, a gener­ alized estimating equation (GEE) model was performed using an exchangeable working correlation structure with robust standard errors. Patient identifier was specified as the clustering variable. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), and independent variables included baseline BCVA, number of injections, treat­ ment switching status, age, and sex. Data collection Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Variables included age, sex, number of outpatient visits, total number of intravitreal injections, baseline and 12-month BCVA, and treatment switching status. BCVA was measured using Snellen charts and converted to logarithm of the minimum angle of reso­ lution (logMAR) units using standardized conversion methods. Visual acuity change (ΔlogMAR) was calcu­ lated as the difference between 12-month and baseline values, with negative values indicating visual improve­ ment. Visual outcomes were additionally categorized as improvement (decrease in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR), sta­ bility (change in BCVA between - 0.1 and + 0.1 logMAR), or deterioration (increase in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR). Sensitivity analysis As a sensitivity analysis, the regression model was repeated after restricting the dataset to one randomly selected eye per patient to assess the robustness of the findings. For subgroup analysis, eyes were stratified according to the median baseline BCVA value (1.0 log­ MAR).

Real-world data, such as those presented in this study, are essential for evaluating how these strategies may be implemented in clinical practice. The difference between the conventional multivariable regression and the GEE analysis is likely attributable to their differing underlying statistical assumptions. Con­ ventional regression assumes that each eye represents an independent observation, whereas the GEE model accounts for the within-patient correlation arising from the inclusion of both eyes from some patients. Failure to account for this correlation may underestimate standard errors, thereby increasing the likelihood of statistically significant findings. Because our study included bilateral observations, the GEE model was considered to provide the more appropriate population-averaged estimates and was therefore regarded as the primary inferential analysis. The strengths of this study include the large sample size and the comprehensive evaluation of treatment bur­ den, switching patterns, and visual outcomes within a single real-world clinical setting. In addition, the use of advanced statistical methods, including GEE analysis and sensitivity analysis restricted to one eye per patient, allowed for more robust estimation of treatment effects by accounting for inter-eye correlation and potential sources of bias. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective design limits causal inference and may introduce selection bias. Second, treatment decisions were not standardized and were made at the discretion of treating physicians, which may have influenced treat­ ment patterns and outcomes. In particular, treatment switching is subject to confounding by indication, as it is preferentially applied to eyes with inadequate response. This limits the ability to disentangle its independent effect on visual outcomes. Although inter-eye correla­ tion was addressed using generalized estimating equation analysis, residual correlation and unmeasured confound­ ing cannot be completely excluded. This may include unmeasured differences in patient demographics, sys­ temic comorbidities, and disease-related characteristics that could influence both treatment patterns and visual outcomes. Residual confounding inherent to the obser­ vational nature of the study cannot be fully ruled out, particularly with respect to treatment switching, which may reflect underlying disease severity and physician decision-making. The timing of treatment switching was not modeled as a time-dependent variable, which may have influenced the observed associations. Furthermore, important systemic factors such as duration of diabe­ tes, glycemic control, and other vascular comorbidities were not included in the analysis. The severity stage of diabetic retinopathy (e.g., non-proliferative versus pro­ liferative diabetic retinopathy) was also not consistently available in the retrospective records and therefore could not be incorporated into the analysis.

chunks.document_content: Background Diabetic macular edema (DME) is becoming one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide with a significant impact on quality of life. The effectiveness of intravitreal (IVT) anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapy has been established by clinical trials and has become the treatment of choice in the majority of DME patients in reducing macular edema and improving visual acuity. Frequent drop-out and discontinuation of treatment are major issues. Lack of compliance can lead to worsening outcomes and be a burden to patients and the healthcare system.
